question: Under a one-step surrogate that makes all curvature beyond the gradient isotropic, what matrix update minimizes the modeled loss change, and does that surrogate make Muon's complete gradient orthogonalization optimal?

key_findings.claim: The paper replaces the exact one-step loss change by an isotropic convex program over a matrix update.
key_findings.evidence: Starting from a per-example Taylor expansion of L(Wu_i), the derivation approximates the Hessian-integral quadratic form by a scalar curvature function H of ||delta W u_i||, drops its dependence on the current activation Wu_i, replaces the empirical inputs by i.i.d. samples zeta from a sphere, and sets Q=-delta W. The resulting model is min_Q -Tr(QG^T)+E[H(||Q zeta||)]. This is a phenomenological surrogate, not an equality for a neural-network step.

key_findings.claim: Within that rotationally invariant surrogate, an optimum can be chosen with the same left and right singular spaces as the gradient.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3.1 fixes the singular values of Q and uses von Neumann's trace inequality to maximize Tr(QG^T) by aligning Q's singular vectors with G. In the generic distinct-singular-value case the alignment is necessary; with degeneracies the proposition asserts existence of an aligned optimum.

key_findings.claim: If x maps to H(sqrt(x)) as a convex function, the optimal update preserves singular-value order while weakly contracting every pairwise singular-value ratio.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 proves sigma_i>=sigma_j implies sigma_i*>=sigma_j* and max(sigma_i*,sigma_j*)/min(sigma_i*,sigma_j*) <= max(sigma_i,sigma_j)/min(sigma_i,sigma_j). Thus the model predicts spectrum homogenization, not a learning rate or absolute update magnitude. The quadratic boundary case H(r)=cr^2 gives Q* proportional to G and therefore equality rather than strict homogenization.

key_findings.claim: Exact gradient orthogonalization is an extreme, generally non-optimal case of the model rather than its default recommendation.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 obtains Q*=r-tilde times msign(G) only for full-column-rank G with m>=n and a convex H whose derivative has a sufficiently wide jump [A,B] at r-tilde. Proposition 3.4 says that for a non-orthonormal G, a scaled matrix-sign optimum requires H to be nondifferentiable at the selected radius. The paper explicitly says real curvature is unlikely to exhibit this exact kink and concludes that partial homogenization is generally preferable.

key_findings.claim: A GPT-2-small probe supports super-quadratic remainder growth over a limited radius range, but it does not test isotropy or optimizer performance.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 measures H(r)/r^2 for ten MLP and ten attention layers using 100 Gaussian perturbation directions, the first 300 C4-newslike validation examples truncated to 100 tokens, and 2,970,000 remainder terms per radius. Fitted exponents 2+alpha range from 2.10 to 2.42 for the shown MLP layers and 2.05 to 2.50 for attention layers. The experiment radially renormalizes every delta W u_i and supplies no directional-variance statistic, error bar, alternative architecture, or trained-optimizer comparison.

key_findings.claim: The paper's own plateau observation conflicts with the global, unconstrained optimization program used by its theorems unless a local radius restriction is added.
key_findings.evidence: The model needs H(r)/r eventually larger than a G-dependent constant so that -Tr(QG^T)+E H(||Qzeta||) does not diverge to -infinity. The same page states that the real loss remainder must eventually plateau at random-predictor loss. A bounded H cannot dominate the linear trace term as ||Q|| grows, yet Equation (2) contains no trust region. The global optimum is therefore a property of the extrapolated coercive H, not of the acknowledged globally realistic H.

anchors.section: Section 2.2, well-posedness requirement and plateau caveat

key_findings.claim: The work establishes conditional geometry inside its surrogate, not that a new spectrum transform improves language-model training.
key_findings.evidence: All optimizer-design implications after Figure 1 are theoretical or prospective. There is no implementation of the convex-program update, no Muon/Adam/Shampoo/PolarGrad training run, no loss-versus-compute comparison, and no ablation of singular-value ordering. The discussion explicitly leaves curvature estimation, layer/time variation, noisy mini-batches, momentum, and GPU solution of Equation (2) to future work.

anchors.section: Section 5, limitations and future optimizer design

method.core_idea: Compress the unknown second- and higher-order response of one matrix-valued neural-network layer into a rotationally invariant scalar function H, then solve the resulting convex matrix program spectrally.
method.mechanism: A per-sample Taylor remainder is approximated by H(||delta W u_i||). Spherical inputs turn its average into E H(||Q zeta||), while the first-order term remains -Tr(QG^T). Rotational invariance and von Neumann's inequality align the update with the gradient's singular spaces. Convexity of H(sqrt(x)) makes the first-order spectral conditions contract singular-value ratios. A wide subgradient interval at a curvature kink lets one choose direction-dependent subgradients that support equal update singular values.
assumptions: The loss depends on the isolated matrix W only through Wu_i; residual connections and other paths are ignored.
The Hessian integral's singular spaces are independent of delta W u_i, so its quadratic form can be replaced by average eigenvalue times squared norm.
Curvature depends on the perturbation only through its Euclidean norm and not on direction or current activation Wu_i.
Layer inputs u_i behave as independent identically distributed samples from a centered sphere.
The scalar H is increasing and sufficiently coercive; for Theorem 1, x->H(sqrt(x)) is convex.
Theorem 2 additionally needs m>=n, full-column-rank G, and a nondifferentiable H with sufficiently small left slope A and sufficiently large right slope B.
The program describes an average single step; it does not model gradient noise, momentum, weight decay, optimizer state, or multi-step convergence.

techniques.role: Retains matrix-input structure while separating the exact first-order gradient term from higher-order curvature.
Replaces directional Hessian and higher-order information by a univariate radial penalty H.
Eliminates the observed activation vectors and makes the surrogate rotationally invariant.
Shows that an optimum can share the gradient's left and right singular spaces.
Uses convexity of H(sqrt(x)) and sphere-coordinate exchangeability to prove spectrum homogenization.
Constructs a scaled matrix-sign optimum from a sufficiently wide subdifferential.
Estimates radial growth exponents from GPT-2-small loss remainders.

evaluations.setting: GPT-2 small, ten MLP layers and ten attention layers, first 300 C4-newslike validation examples truncated to 100 tokens, 100 Gaussian perturbation directions
evaluations.metric: Slope of H(r)/r^2 and fitted exponent 2+alpha from r=10^0.5
evaluations.result: Displayed exponents span 2.10-2.42 for MLP layers and 2.05-2.50 for attention layers; the curves are nearly quadratic at small radius and usually grow faster after roughly r=10^0.5
evaluations.baseline: Purely quadratic curvature would keep H(r)/r^2 constant and have exponent 2

evaluations.metric: Pairwise singular-value ratio of the optimal update relative to the gradient
evaluations.result: Every optimal ratio is no larger than its gradient counterpart while singular-value ordering is preserved
evaluations.baseline: H(r)=cr^2 gives Q proportional to G and no ratio change

evaluations.result: Each sigma_j* solves (sigma_j*)^3+D sigma_j*=n(n+2)sigma_j/(8c), with D=(1/2)sum_i(sigma_i*)^2, yielding strict ratio contraction for unequal positive gradient singular values

evaluations.setting: Convex H with a derivative jump [A,B] at r-tilde, m>=n, and full-column-rank G
evaluations.metric: Existence and necessity of a scaled matrix-sign optimum
evaluations.result: For unspecified sufficiently small A and large B, Q*=r-tilde msign(G) is optimal; if H is differentiable at the selected radius and G has unequal singular values, exact orthogonalization cannot be optimal
evaluations.baseline: Smooth super-quadratic H yields partial homogenization rather than equal singular values

evaluations.metric: Training loss, validation loss, compute, or wall-clock performance
evaluations.baseline: No Adam, Muon, Shampoo, SOAP, PolarGrad, or learned spectrum-transform control is run in this paper

limitations: Author-stated: the model is meant to describe an average single iteration, not any particular stochastic training step.
Author-stated: dependence of the Taylor remainder on the current activation Wu_i is dropped.
Author-stated: residual connections are ignored in the layer-isolation argument.
Author-stated: the practical curvature function eventually plateaus, whereas the global convex program needs coercive growth to possess an optimum.
Author-stated: exact orthogonalization requires an extreme derivative kink that is unlikely to occur in practice.
Author-stated: Theorem 2 assumes m>=n; the m<n extension is left as an approximate future result.
Author-stated: Theorem 2's proof is nonconstructive and supplies no usable thresholds for how small A or how large B must be.
Author-stated: the model omits mini-batch noise, momentum, layer/time variation of H, and multi-step convergence.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 1 measures radial remainder growth but never tests the central directional-isotropy, Hessian-eigenvector-independence, or spherical-activation assumptions.
Reviewer-identified: per-example renormalization of delta W u_i isolates H as a function of radius but no longer represents one common matrix perturbation acting naturally on all examples.
Reviewer-identified: evidence comes from GPT-2 small, one validation subset, and displayed layer probes without seeds, uncertainty, checkpoints, or alternative architectures.
Reviewer-identified: the spectrum theorem does not determine step size, and the paper never solves Equation (2) at training scale or tests whether its transform improves Muon.
Reviewer-identified: isotropy is particularly tensioned by direct Muon analyses that attribute gains to low-rank gradients, low-rank Hessians, block structure, or anisotropic constraints.
Reviewer-identified: preserving singular-value order is presented as a design requirement, but no experiment shows that nonmonotone Newton-Schulz approximations harm optimization.
failure_modes: If curvature is anisotropic or correlated with the update direction, the radial H can recommend the wrong singular spaces as well as the wrong spectrum.
If activations occupy a structured non-spherical subspace, E H(||Qzeta||) misweights directions relevant to the actual data.
If realistic H plateaus and Q is unconstrained, the surrogate objective can run to -infinity rather than select an update.
A smooth power-law H predicts only partial homogenization, so exact Muon orthogonalization can oversuppress genuinely informative large singular directions.
Rank-deficient gradients and wide matrices fall outside the exact Theorem 2 setup or require the paper's unproved extension.
A spectrum transformation implemented by a nonmonotone low-degree polynomial can invert nearby singular-value order even when the ideal model preserves it.
A curvature function estimated at one layer, radius range, or checkpoint can be obsolete at another layer or later in training.
The computational cost of estimating H and solving the full convex spectral problem can erase the practical advantage over Muon's inexpensive approximate matrix sign.
reusable_insights: Separate the question of singular-space alignment from the question of singular-value transformation when analyzing matrix optimizers.
A radial penalty whose squared-radius form is convex naturally contracts spectral ratios; this supplies a generic route to partial conditioning without assuming full orthogonalization.
Exact equalization often signals a nonsmooth constraint or kink, whereas smooth penalties usually produce graded shrinkage.
Empirical support for an isotropic surrogate should report directional dispersion and alignment, not only a radial mean curve.
Any globally optimized Taylor surrogate should include a trust region or a demonstrably coercive remainder; local empirical curvature cannot safely be extrapolated to arbitrary update norms.
Optimizer implementations that approximate spectral maps should check monotonicity over the singular-value range actually encountered.
open_questions: Does directional curvature at real language-model checkpoints become isotropic after conditioning on perturbation norm, and with what variance across directions?
Can the model be made well posed with an explicit trust region while retaining the alignment and homogenization theorems?
What finite, constructive slope interval [A,B] is enough for approximate rather than exact orthogonalization?
Can H be estimated cheaply online per layer and converted into a monotone GPU-friendly spectrum map?
Does the predicted partially homogenized update outperform exact Muon under matched FLOPs and tuned learning rates?
How do mini-batch noise, momentum, weight decay, residual paths, and m<n layers alter the optimal spectrum?
Can anisotropic or low-rank curvature models explain when the isotropic prescription fails?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Gradient Orthogonalization for Deep Learning via Non-Euclidean Trust-Region Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Kovalev derives Muon as stochastic non-Euclidean trust-region gradient descent under a matrix spectral-norm trust region and proves convergence results. The target instead derives a one-step high-order-curvature surrogate and asks how far the gradient spectrum should be homogenized; it offers no multi-step convergence guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: PolarGrad: A Class of Matrix-Gradient Optimizers from a Unifying Preconditioning Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: PolarGrad distinguishes vector preconditioning for curvature anisotropy from matrix preconditioning for gradient anisotropy, includes a scaled Muon instance, and reports matrix and language-model experiments outperforming Adam and Muon. The target supplies a radial-curvature rationale for singular-space alignment and a negative result about exact equalization, but does not implement its proposed optimum.

competitive_landscape.title: Muon Optimizes Under Spectral Norm Constraints
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen, Li, and Liu identify Muon with a nuclear-norm Lion-K update and analyze its implicit spectral-norm constraint, especially with decoupled weight decay. The target studies optimal one-step update singular values under isotropic high-order curvature and omits weight decay, so it addresses a different object than the induced weight constraint.

competitive_landscape.title: Implicit Bias of Spectral Descent and Muon on Multiclass Separable Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Fan, Schmidt, and Thrampoulidis characterize normalized and momentum steepest descent, including Muon, as converging to spectral-norm max-margin classifiers on multiclass separable data. The target's result is a one-step spectrum prescription for a general matrix layer, not a trajectory-level implicit-bias result for classification.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Convergence Analysis of Muon
competitive_landscape.difference: Shen et al. compare Muon with gradient descent, prove convergence rates, and attribute advantages to low-rank Hessian structure with supporting experiments. The target assumes isotropic curvature and proves a conditional single-step optimum, so the two accounts make materially different structural commitments that need a common empirical test.

competitive_landscape.title: Lions and Muons: Optimization via Stochastic Frank-Wolfe under Heavy-Tailed Noise
competitive_landscape.difference: Sfyraki and Wang interpret Lion and weight-decayed Muon as stochastic Frank-Wolfe, prove Frank-Wolfe-gap and KKT guarantees, and extend the analysis to heavy-tailed noise. The target ignores stochastic noise and constraints and instead derives partial-versus-complete spectrum homogenization from an averaged Taylor remainder.

competitive_landscape.title: An Exploration of Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent: Muon and its Many Variants
competitive_landscape.difference: Crawshaw et al. organize Muon variants by layer norms, aggregation, normalization, and momentum, and find Muon learning-rate sensitivity while MuonMax and Momo variants are more robust. The target predicts a monotone, partially homogenizing spectral transform but does not compare it with these experimentally tested alternatives.

competitive_landscape.title: The Polar Express: Optimal Matrix Sign Methods and Their Application to the Muon Algorithm
competitive_landscape.difference: Amsel et al. optimize the GPU approximation of the matrix sign itself, prove minimax polynomial error properties, handle bfloat16, and report GPT-2 validation gains inside Muon. The target challenges whether the exact matrix sign is the right mathematical update at all and redirects attention from approximation error to choosing a nonuniform spectrum.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a new isotropic-curvature convex model that explains why matrix-gradient methods preserve gradient singular spaces, proves that super-quadratic curvature favors spectrum homogenization, and identifies a sharp phase-transition condition under which Muon's complete orthogonalization is optimal.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Equation (2), Proposition 3.1, Theorem 1, Theorem 2, and Proposition 3.4 establish these statements inside the surrogate; Figure 1 supplies a limited radial-growth probe on GPT-2 small.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the particular high-order radial surrogate and its partial-homogenization/necessary-kink result. Earlier exact-version primary work already explains Muon through non-Euclidean trust regions, spectral constraints, max-margin implicit bias, stochastic Frank-Wolfe, low-rank Hessian convergence, structured preconditioning, and matrix-sign numerics. The target therefore does not provide Muon's first theoretical foundation. Its most distinctive contribution is the negative claim that exact orthogonalization is generally too extreme, but that claim remains model-conditional and empirically untested; moreover, the acknowledged plateau of real H makes the global unconstrained surrogate ill posed without a trust region.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text review covered all 19 pages of the pinned arXiv:2511.00674v1 paper: derivation, all assumptions, Figure 1 and its sampling arithmetic, Theorems 1-2, Propositions 3.1 and 3.4, the quartic worked example, every proof in Section 4, discussion, footnotes, and all references. The full-text pin was checked verbatim: 19/19 pages have usable text; PDF SHA-256 27a2b7c13d0107ffe33ecc3c42da5f2af83c25784f061d6380940f2145ef4261 and text SHA-256 5057cf8585aa1d68959e82d6b5d46eeea5ff878fe5109bc0f782b59edd53654c.
